title: Why & For Whom

learn.summary: Every piece of writing is an answer to two questions: who is this for, and what should change in their head after reading it? William Zinsser opens On Writing Well by insisting the product a writer sells is not the subject but 'who he is' — a clear mind on the page. Before drafting anything, name the reader and the single thing you want them to know, feel, or do.

do: For your next piece of writing, write one sentence at the top before you start: 'After reading this, [specific reader] will [specific outcome].'

children.title: Knowing Your Reader

learn.summary: Composition courses drill the 'rhetorical situation': every text has an audience with existing knowledge, attention limits, and reasons to stop reading. Writing for 'everyone' produces prose for no one — the busy executive, the curious novice, and the skeptical expert need different openings, different evidence, different lengths. Zinsser's twist: paradoxically, you write best for others when you first write to please one demanding reader, yourself.

do: Rewrite one paragraph you have already written for two different readers (an expert and a newcomer) and note every change you made.

children.title: Purpose Before Prose

learn.summary: Classical rhetoric sorts writing by aim — to inform, persuade, entertain, or move to action — and each aim implies different choices about structure and evidence. Most muddled documents are muddled because they try to do three of these at once. Decide your primary purpose first; a memo that must inform and persuade should still know which master it serves when the two conflict.

do: Take your three most recent emails or documents and label each with its primary purpose in one word; rewrite any where you cannot decide.

children.title: Writing as Thinking

learn.summary: Zinsser: 'Writing is thinking on paper.' The act of forcing thoughts into sequential sentences exposes gaps that felt like knowledge while they stayed vague — which is why explaining an idea in writing is the fastest way to discover you do not understand it. Treat confused drafts as good news: the confusion was already there, and now it is visible and fixable.

do: Pick one idea you think you understand and write a 200-word explanation for a smart 12-year-old; list every point where you got stuck.

children.title: Reading Like a Writer

learn.summary: Writers train by reverse-engineering prose they admire: not what it says but how it works — where the writer entered the subject, how long the sentences run, what got left out. Francine Prose built a whole book (Reading Like a Writer) on this close-reading habit, and it is the cheapest writing instruction available. One paragraph studied hard teaches more than ten read passively.

do: Copy out, by hand, one paragraph you love this week, then annotate it: sentence lengths, verb choices, and where it surprised you.
